documents.title: Regulation for the Use of Generative AI Systems with Institutional Data
documents.summary: A university regulation that governs how generative AI may be used with public and protected institutional data. It allows any AI tool for public data, limits protected data to offline or vetted tools, and sets vendor and procurement rules. It says almost nothing about teaching or coursework.
documents.stance_why: The regulation says the University 'allows Generative AI tools to be utilized effectively' and 'encourages exploration of these products or services', with conditions on data: 'Any generative AI product or service is allowed' for public data and only vetted tools for protected data. That is permission with conditions, not delegation.

units.why: The Purpose section says it states 'the University's requirements regarding the use of Generative AI tools with public and institutional data'. This sets the regulation's scope, so informs, general, P61.
units.anchor: state the University’s requirements regarding the use of Generative AI tools with public and institutional
units.resolution_why: Only coder A found this (as P56, policy-evolution). The source sentence is the regulation's purpose and scope statement, which fits P61 (policy scope) better than P56, so it is kept as P61.

units.why: States the regulation's aims: 'safeguard academic integrity, protect intellectual property, and ensure compliance'. A principles preamble for institution-wide responsible use, so P56.
units.anchor: guidelines that safeguard academic integrity, protect intellectual property, and ensure compliance with legal and regulatory

units.why: Says the University 'allows Generative AI tools to be utilized effectively'. A university-level default of allowing AI use, so P02 (permit by default).
units.anchor: the University allows Generative AI tools to be utilized effectively without compromising the integrity of
units.resolution_why: A coded may/P02; B coded informs/P56. The source says 'the University allows Generative AI tools to be utilized effectively', which grants permission, so may/permit and P02 (permit by default), not a framework statement.

units.why: Defines generative AI as a type of AI that 'produces new content'. A definition that sets what the regulation covers, so P61.
units.anchor: Generative AI is a type of artificial intelligence that produces new content

units.why: The University 'encourages exploration of these products or services'. A welcoming default stance toward AI use, so P02.
units.anchor: East Carolina University encourages exploration of these products or services

units.why: Requires individuals to 'remain cognizant of data being provided to these tools'. This is a data-protection duty, so P50 and not P02. Final codes follow the resolution_why.
units.anchor: individuals must remain cognizant of data being provided to these tools
units.resolution_why: A coded phase general, B during-work. 'individuals must remain cognizant of data being provided to these tools' applies while using the tools, so during-work.

units.why: Individuals must 'abide by copyright laws' when using these tools. Copyright compliance of AI use fits P52 (licensing and copyright). Final codes follow the resolution_why.
units.anchor: abide by copyright laws, compliance regulations, Employee Code of Conduct, and Student Code of Conduct
units.resolution_why: A coded general/neutral, B during-work/restrict. The sentence tells users to 'abide by copyright laws, compliance regulations' and the codes of conduct while using the tools; it adds no AI-specific limit, so during-work with unit_stance neutral.

units.why: Violators 'will be subject to the penalties outlined in' the codes and the Student Conduct Process. Misuse is handled through existing conduct processes, so P36. P37 needs specific penalties, which are not stated.
units.anchor: found to be in violation of this regulation will be subject to the penalties outlined

units.why: 'Any generative AI product or service is allowed' for Level 1 public data. A permission rule about which tools may be used, so P02 (default permit) for public data. Final codes follow the resolution_why.
units.anchor: Any generative AI product or service is allowed.
units.resolution_why: A coded general/P02, B during-work/P50. 'Any generative AI product or service is allowed' for Level 1 public data is a permission, so P02 (the data-protection content sits in the neighbouring Level 2-4 unit, which is P50). Phase is during-work because it governs which tools may be used.

units.why: For protected data, only offline or local tools or tools on the Sensitive Data list are 'authorized'. It restricts use to vetted tools, so P50 (prefer vetted tools). P17 does not fit because no course tool is provided.
units.anchor: Only generative AI products or services that are run offline and locally on ECU managed

units.why: Warns that other tools 'could violate state or federal statutes such as HIPAA and FERPA'. This is the rationale for data protection, P50.
units.anchor: could violate state or federal statutes such as HIPAA and FERPA

units.why: Listed tools 'will clarify its compatibility with various data levels'. Describes how approved tools are documented for users, part of vetted-tool guidance, P50.
units.anchor: Each generative AI product or service listed on the website will clarify its compatibility with
units.resolution_why: Only coder A found this. The source says 'Each generative AI product or service listed on the website will clarify its compatibility with various data levels', which is a real procedural statement about tool vetting, so it is kept.

units.why: 'Passphrases must never be used' with tools not on single sign-on. A prohibition that protects credentials, so P50.
units.anchor: Passphrases must never be used with generative AI products or services

units.why: 'Never share any sensitive, personal, or institutional data' with tools considered public facing. Data protection, P50.
units.anchor: Never share any sensitive, personal, or institutional data other than what is outlined

units.why: Tells users to 'Review and be familiar with ECU’s data classification standards'. A practice recommendation for data protection, P50.
units.anchor: Review and be familiar with ECU’s data classification standards
units.resolution_why: A coded phase general, B before-course. 'Review and be familiar with ECU's data classification standards' is a general recommended practice, not course set-up, so general.

units.why: People working with institutional data 'must be aware of HIPAA, FERPA, GDPR, GLBA'. A legal-awareness duty tied to data privacy, P50.
units.anchor: must be aware of HIPAA, FERPA, GDPR, GLBA, and other federal, state, or university regulations

units.why: Says generative AI is 'a prominent driver of phishing scams' and requires following security practices and reporting. AI-enabled security threats fit no type, so UNCOVERED.
units.anchor: must be followed and any suspicious messages reported to phish@ecu.edu
units.uncovered_note: AI-enabled phishing and information-security practices: follow ITCS best practices and report suspicious messages (cybersecurity, not data privacy or bias).

units.why: "The approval of a tool does not override any governing data laws" and a data steward, IRB or Data Use Agreement can bar AI use. Deferring to IRB and data-use-agreement rules matches P62.
units.anchor: you may not use generative AI tools even if they are approved herein
units.resolution_why: A anchored on the data steward/IRB clause (general), B on 'you may not use generative AI tools even if they are approved herein' (during-work). Both coded must-not, P62, restrict. The prohibition applies at the moment of use, so during-work, and B's anchor states the rule more directly.

units.why: Acquisition of AI products 'must comply with the Software and Data Collection Services Acquisition Regulation'. Institutional review of AI purchases, P65.
units.anchor: acquisition of generative AI products or services must comply with the Software and Data Collection

units.why: Vendors approved for Level 2-4 data 'must adhere to security industry best practices'. Vendor requirements, P65.
units.anchor: Vendors of any generative AI product or service who are approved to process ECU’s Level

units.why: Safeguards must 'apply to the generative AI models trained with university data'. A limit on vendors' handling of university data, P65.
units.anchor: must also apply to the generative AI models trained with university data

units.why: 'Available and approved software ... can be found' on the licensed software site. It points users to licensed tools, so P50 (prefer vetted or licensed tools). P17 does not fit because no specific tool is named.
units.anchor: Available and approved software at the University can be found via the Licensed ECU Software

units.why: 'Termination of a vendor agreement must adhere to any applicable contracts'. A vendor agreement rule, P65.
units.anchor: Termination of a vendor agreement must adhere to any applicable contracts.
units.resolution_why: Only coder A found this. 'Termination of a vendor agreement must adhere to any applicable contracts' is a requirement on vendor agreements in the regulation, so it is kept.

units.why: 'No exceptions to this regulation will be approved until a contract is in place'. A contract precondition on AI vendors, P65.
units.anchor: No exceptions to this regulation will be approved until a contract is in place

units.why: 'Any procurement ... must go through the Technology Purchase Process'. Procurement review of AI vendors, P65.
units.anchor: must go through the Technology Purchase Process

units.why: 'All faculty, staff, and students are required to follow' the regulation. It sets who the regulation binds, so P56. Final codes follow the resolution_why.
units.anchor: All faculty, staff, and students are required to follow the Institutional Data and AI regulation.

documents.unit: Office for Faculty Excellence / ECU Libraries
documents.title: Generative AI in the Classroom & Research: Classroom Best Practices
documents.summary: Library guide that tells faculty they decide how AI is used in their classes and offers three adapted syllabus statements. It also covers citation, copyright, hallucination, ethics and sample AI assignments, much of it drawn from ChatGPT output.
documents.stance_why: The guide states 'faculty have the ability to determine the extent to which artificial intelligence may be used in the classroom' and offers 'three scenarios ... faculty can choose from' (prohibited, prior permission, with acknowledgement). It sets no single rule itself, so it delegates and lists tiers.

units.why: Faculty 'have the ability to determine the extent to which artificial intelligence may be used in the classroom'. The rule is set by each instructor, so P04.
units.anchor: faculty have the ability to determine the extent to which artificial intelligence may be used

units.why: Policies 'should be in keeping with the University's Academic Integrity policies'. An alignment requirement on instructor policies. P56 (institution framework) fits better than P04, which covers who decides and not alignment.
units.anchor: Policies should be in keeping with the University's Academic Integrity policies
units.resolution_why: A coded P56, B coded P04. 'Policies should be in keeping with the University's Academic Integrity policies' binds instructor-set rules to the university framework rather than saying who decides, so P56 (the instructor-discretion rule is the previous unit, P04).

units.why: Offers three syllabus scenarios that 'faculty can choose from'. Named categories of use that faculty pick from, so P05 (tiers) rather than P04.
units.anchor: three scenarios and examples of syllabus language faculty can choose from

units.why: Under the Academic Integrity policy, 'using an AI tool, if prohibited by the instructor, is considered an academic integrity violation'. Misuse is classed as misconduct, P36. Final codes follow the resolution_why.
units.anchor: using an AI tool, if prohibited by the instructor, is considered an academic integrity violation
units.resolution_why: A coded unit_stance prohibit, B restrict. The violation applies only 'if prohibited by the instructor', so the ban is conditional on the instructor's choice: restrict.

units.why: Presenting another's 'language, structure, ideas' as one's own without citing is 'plagiarism'. A definition of misuse as plagiarism, P36.
units.anchor: using language, structure, ideas and/or thoughts of another and adopting the same as one’s own

units.why: 'We strongly recommend faculty remind their students to always cite when using any AI tool'. A recommendation that students cite AI use, so P24 (disclose with each submission). Final codes follow the resolution_why.
units.anchor: We strongly recommend faculty remind their students to always cite when using any AI tool
units.resolution_why: A coded unit_stance require, B encourage. 'We strongly recommend faculty remind their students to always cite' is a recommendation, not a requirement, so should/encourage.

units.why: The Office of Student Rights and Responsibilities provides 'Academic Syllabus Statements' for syllabi. This is support for faculty, P63. P09 does not fit because no syllabus statement is required.
units.anchor: has created several Academic Syllabus Statements that you can add to your syllabi

units.why: "even if permitted by the instructor, using an AI tool without properly citing its use is also plagiarism" makes non-disclosure the violation: P28.
units.anchor: by the instructor, using an AI tool without properly citing its use is also plagiarism
units.resolution_why: A coded must, B informs. 'even if permitted by the instructor, using an AI tool without properly citing its use is also plagiarism' classifies uncited use as misconduct, like the neighbouring P36 definitions, so informs with P28 (nondisclosure is the violation) and restrict.

units.why: 'Please modify these statements to suit the needs of your course'. Invites per-course adaptation by the instructor, P04.
units.anchor: Please modify these statements to suit the needs of your course.

units.why: The 'USE PROHIBITED' statement bars tools like ChatGPT 'on assignments in this course'. A ban on graded work, P01.
units.anchor: Students are not allowed to use advanced automated tools
units.resolution_why: A coded during-work, B course-start. The template bans AI 'on assignments in this course', so the rule governs the work itself: during-work.

units.why: "complete each assignment without substantive assistance from others, including automated tools" bars AI from doing the submitted work. P19 chosen because it treats the tool as a source of assistance on submitted work; P45 (AI as collaborator) fits less since it is a ban, not a collaboration rule.
units.anchor: complete each assignment without substantive assistance from others, including automated tools
units.resolution_why: A coded should/P29, B must-not/P19. The template says each student is 'expected to complete each assignment without substantive assistance from others, including automated tools'. This is a ban on having AI do the submitted work, which is P19, and it binds the student in the template, so must-not.

units.why: Template 2 allows AI "if instructor permission is obtained in advance", so students must ask first: P10. Final codes follow the resolution_why.
units.anchor: on assignments in this course if instructor permission is obtained in advance
units.resolution_why: A coded may/P04, B must/P10. AI is allowed 'if instructor permission is obtained in advance'. The student may use AI, and only after asking, so may with P10 (ask first). P04 would apply to who decides, which is the earlier unit.

units.why: 'Unless given permission ... each student is expected to complete each assignment without substantive assistance'. States the rule when permission is absent, so P06. Final codes follow the resolution_why.
units.anchor: Unless given permission to use those tools, each student is expected to complete each assignment
units.resolution_why: A coded should, B must; both P06. 'Unless given permission to use those tools, each student is expected to complete each assignment without substantive assistance' is the binding default in a syllabus template, so must.

units.why: If permission is granted, tools 'must be properly documented and credited'. Disclosure with the submission, P24. Final codes follow the resolution_why.
units.anchor: they must be properly documented and credited
units.resolution_why: A coded unit_stance require, B permit. The documentation duty is a condition on permitted use; AI use is not required, so permit.

units.why: 'Students should seek out the appropriate source (e.g., MLA, APA) and cite in the most correct format'. Citation format instruction, P24. It does not require prompt or output, so not P25. Final codes follow the resolution_why.
units.anchor: cite in the most correct format according to the style guide
units.resolution_why: A coded unit_stance require, B permit. Citing format is a condition on permitted use, so permit.

units.why: Students 'must also include a brief (2-3 sentences) description of how they used the tool'. A written account of use, P26. Final codes follow the resolution_why.
units.anchor: students must also include a brief (2-3 sentences) description of how they used the tool
units.resolution_why: A coded unit_stance require, B permit. The 2-3 sentence description is a condition on permitted use, so permit.

units.why: The 'USE WITH ACKNOWLEDGEMENT' statement allows tools 'if that use is properly documented and credited'. Default permit with disclosure, P02.
units.anchor: allowed to use advanced automated tools

units.why: The guide suggests assignments like "Have students use an AI-powered image recognition tool to classify images", building course work around AI tools: P35. Final codes follow the resolution_why.
units.anchor: Have students use an AI-powered image recognition tool to classify images
units.policy: The guide offers ChatGPT-generated assignment ideas in which students use or build AI-powered tools, such as image recognition, chatbot development and comparing AI grading to human grading.
units.resolution_why: A anchored on the chatbot item, B on the image-recognition item; both are items of the same ChatGPT-generated assignment list (P35). The items are merged into one unit with a normalized policy. A's separate unit for the automated-grading item is folded in here.

units.why: Says such assignments 'can help students develop a better understanding of how AI works'. A rationale for teaching with AI, P44.
units.anchor: help students develop a better understanding of how AI works and how it can be
units.resolution_why: A coded general, B before-course. 'These assignments can help students develop a better understanding of how AI works' is a rationale, so general.

units.why: ChatGPT's list of faculty uses says 'AI-powered tools can be used to grade assignments and provide feedback'. Instructor AI use in teaching work, P59. It does not decide final grades, so not P46. Final codes follow the resolution_why.
units.anchor: AI-powered tools can be used to grade assignments and provide feedback to students
units.resolution_why: A coded may/permit/P59, B informs/neutral/P59. The sentence is part of a ChatGPT-generated answer reproduced on the guide ('AI-powered tools can be used to grade assignments'); it describes a possible use rather than granting permission, so informs/neutral.

units.why: A ChatGPT answer reproduced in the guide says 'AI-powered chatbots can be used to provide students with answers to frequently asked questions'. It describes an instructor use of AI, a fact rather than a grant, so informs, P59.
units.anchor: AI-powered chatbots can be used to provide students with answers to frequently asked questions
units.resolution_why: Only coder A found this (as may/permit). It sits in the same reproduced ChatGPT list as the grading item, which the reconciliation codes informs/neutral for consistency. Kept as a statement about faculty use of AI.

units.why: A reproduced ChatGPT answer says 'AI-powered virtual tutors can be used to provide students with immediate feedback and guidance'. It describes an instructor use of AI; the guide does not provide a tool, so P59 informs, not P17.
units.anchor: AI-powered virtual tutors can be used to provide students with immediate feedback and guidance
units.resolution_why: Only coder A found this (as may/encourage/P17). The guide does not provide or sanction a tutor tool, so P17 does not fit; it is a description of faculty use like the grading item. Kept as informs/P59.

units.why: A reproduced ChatGPT answer says 'AI can be used by faculty to conduct research, by analyzing data, identifying patterns'. This describes a faculty research use, so informs, P62.
units.anchor: AI can be used by faculty to conduct research, by analyzing data, identifying patterns, and
units.resolution_why: Only coder A found this (as may/permit). It is part of the reproduced ChatGPT list, so informs/neutral is used for consistency. Kept as a statement about research use.

units.why: The ChatGPT answer urges one to 'carefully consider the potential ethical implications' and use AI transparently. An ethics concern, P53.
units.anchor: it is important to carefully consider the potential ethical implications of using AI in education

units.why: Names 'Unfair Advantage' leading to academic dishonesty as an ethical implication. A harm and fairness concern, P53.
units.anchor: could lead to academic dishonesty, and ultimately undermine the integrity of the educational system

units.why: 'AI tools may require access to student data, which raises privacy concerns'. A privacy concern, P50.
units.anchor: AI tools may require access to student data, which raises privacy concerns

units.why: AI models 'can perpetuate biases that exist in the data'. A bias concern, P53.
units.anchor: they can perpetuate biases that exist in the data

units.why: A lack of transparency makes it 'difficult to understand how decisions are being made'. An ethics concern, P53.
units.anchor: This lack of transparency could make it difficult to understand how decisions are being made
units.resolution_why: Only coder A found this. 'This lack of transparency could make it difficult to understand how decisions are being made' is a stated ethical concern about AI, in the same reproduced answer as the bias and privacy units, so it is kept.

units.why: Recommends 'being transparent about the use of AI, ensuring that AI-powered tools are fair and unbiased, and protecting student privacy'. Mitigation steps, P53.
units.anchor: being transparent about the use of AI, ensuring that AI-powered tools are fair and unbiased,
units.resolution_why: Only coder A found this. 'being transparent about the use of AI, ensuring that AI-powered tools are fair and unbiased, and protecting student privacy' is a recommended mitigation in the reproduced answer, so it is kept.

units.why: 'Citing ChatGPT ... will allow your work to remain transparent'. Advises citing AI, P24. Final codes follow the resolution_why.
units.anchor: Citing ChatGPT and other generative AI will allow your work to remain transparent
units.resolution_why: A coded unit_stance require, B encourage. 'Citing ChatGPT and other generative AI will allow your work to remain transparent' recommends citing; AI use itself is neither required nor encouraged, only allowed with citation, so should/permit.

units.why: "If generative AI is used in research, best practice would dictate to mention the use of this tool in the narrative" concerns AI in research writing: P62. Final codes follow the resolution_why.
units.anchor: is used in research, best practice would dictate to mention the use of this tool
units.resolution_why: A coded P24/require, B P62/encourage. The sentence is 'If generative AI is used in research, best practice would dictate to mention the use of this tool in the narrative'. Its scope is research, so P62 is where a reader would look; disclosure is a condition on allowed use, so permit.

units.why: States the Copyright Office position that AI-generated texts 'are not eligible for copyright protection'. Copyright of AI output, P52.
units.anchor: texts and images solely or primarily generated by AI are not eligible for copyright protection

units.why: Federal Register guidance 'gives instructions on filling out the copyright registration forms to acknowledge the role of AI'. Copyright registration disclosure, P52.
units.anchor: instructions on filling out the copyright registration forms to acknowledge the role of AI

units.why: Defines hallucination as 'complete fabrication of information'. AI output can be wrong, P31.
units.anchor: Hallucination refers to the phenomenon involving the complete fabrication of information by generative artificial intelligence
units.resolution_why: Only coder A found this. 'Hallucination refers to the phenomenon involving the complete fabrication of information by generative artificial intelligence' defines the risk behind the instructor caution unit, so it is kept as informs.

units.why: 'Instructors should practice caution when permitting students to rely on AI for evidence-based assignments'. Advice grounded in unreliable output, P31.
units.anchor: Instructors should practice caution when permitting students to rely on AI for evidence-based assignments
units.resolution_why: A coded unit_stance restrict, B neutral. 'Instructors should practice caution when permitting students to rely on AI for evidence-based assignments' counsels limiting reliance, so restrict.

units.why: 'ChatGPT has been known to fabricate references'. States that AI output can be false, P31.
units.anchor: ChatGPT has been known to fabricate references for sources

notes: Only two university-layer documents; no school, computing or course documents found. The library guide reproduces ChatGPT-generated text (assignment ideas, Q&A); those passages are coded informs/neutral where they only describe possible uses. The Level 1 permission repeated in the regulation's classification table is skipped as a repeat. The phishing/security unit is UNCOVERED (cybersecurity).
